 In today’s CEO Daily: The character debate takes center stage.
 The big leadership story: Nvidia dismisses the possibility of Jensen Huang’s return. 
 The markets: Stocks rebound on Nvidia’s solid earnings. 
 Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune .
 Good morning. Moments before I interviewed Bristol Myers Squibb CEO Chris Boerner on stage at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum yesterday, a news alert flashed across my phone: The United States had officially lost its measles elimination status, a distinction it had held for more than 25 years. More than 5,400 cases have been reported this year alone under an administration that has fired scientists, disregarded public health protocols, and undermined faith in vaccines.
 Recommended Video 
 I asked Boerner, whose drug company does not make the vaccine, what he made of the news. “Very troubling,” he said, noting that America’s enviable ecosystem in biotechnology and pharmaceuticals is a benefit, not a birthright. “It rests on respect for science.”
 That fireside chat took place around the same time that Jensen Huang said he’d be “honored” to return as CEO of Nvidia, as if multiple affairs and potential security violations paled next to the “outpouring of calls” for him to return. The board declined . Good call.
 My conversations over the past two days reinforced that character matters, in leadership and in life. Rocket Companies founder and chairman Dan Gilbert talked about his extensive investments in transforming downtown Detroit—including The Department at Hudson’s Detroit, where the event was held. He made a compelling case for “more-than-profit” businesses that deliver financially while contributing to the communities in which they operate. He also talked about how his stroke shifted his priorities as a leader and what it will take to realize his dream of making Detroit—and Cleveland—two of the world’s top cities. As for the midterms, Gilbert said, “I hope these guys can shake hands and figure out how to get things done.”
 That sentiment was echoed by former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, a Democrat, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a Republican. Here is a link to our conversation. Both politicians suggested creating ethics laws that would require politicians to put their assets in a blind trust and ban stock trading and investments in prediction markets. 
 Christie declared that “the Trump era is over.” He cited opportunities for bipartisan things to get done. They both predicted that character will be the deciding issue in 2028, or as Christie said, “a president who stands for much more than GDP.” 
 “America needs to close this chapter of pitting one American against the other,” Emanuel said.
 Government matters, but tackling tough problems is what leaders do. Optum CEO Patrick Conway knows that he’s in a health services industry that’s not loved, where customers struggle to pay. Having held senior roles at a health insurer, a hospital system, and in government, he knows that “the system doesn’t work today,” but he’s optimistic that digitization and simplification could transform the patient experience. One reason he continues to work weekends as a practicing physician is that he wants to understand how issues like affordability are affecting patients and “ prevent those stories from occurring in the future.”
 Contact CEO Daily via Diane Brady at diane.brady@fortune.com 
 Top leadership news
 Nvidia chair says board does not plan to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO 
 On Nvidia’s first earnings call since Huang resigned, Chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate him and would not take questions about his departure or the ongoing investigation into his conduct. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, above Wall Street estimates, but analysts did not ask about its sales through Singapore or a reported SEC investigation into possibly misguiding investors. 
 DoorDash’s bid for Instacart puts board ties in focus 
 DoorDash has agreed to buy grocery-delivery rival Instacart for $17 billion, and partners at one investment firm, Sequoia Capital, sit on both companies’ boards. Fortune found similar ties at other investment firms, and legal experts say these arrangements can make rivals less willing to compete and more likely to merge. 
 Fund managers make their biggest cut to tech investments since 2006 
 Fund managers reduced their exposure to tech stocks by the most since June 2006, according to Bank of America’s latest survey. Some 52% expect at least one major cloud company to cut capital spending within six months, despite Wall Street forecasts that spending will rise sharply next year. 
 The markets
 S&P 500 futures are up 0.66% this morning. The last session closed down 1.03%. The STOXX Europe 600 was up 0.1%% in early trading. The U.K.’s FTSE 100 was down 0.29% in early trading. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up 0.28%. South Korea’s KOSPI was up 1.99%. China’s CSI 300 was up 0.18%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was down 0.91%. India’s NIFTY 50 was down 0.63% today. Bitcoin is at $64k.
